facts.title: Named From The German
facts.text: The name "zinc" comes from the German word Zink, popularized by the alchemist and physician Paracelsus in the 16th century. It likely refers to the pointed, tooth-like (Zinke means "prong" or "tine") shape of the crystals that form when the molten metal solidifies. Although the pure metal was isolated relatively late in Europe, the word entered chemistry long before zinc was recognized as a distinct element.

facts.title: India Smelted It First
facts.text: While Europeans were still puzzling over it, metallurgists in India were already producing metallic zinc on an industrial scale by around the 12th century at Zawar in Rajasthan. They used clever downward-distillation retorts to capture zinc vapor, which boils off at only 907 C and would otherwise escape as gas. The German chemist Andreas Marggraf is usually credited with isolating zinc scientifically in 1746, centuries after these Indian smelters.

facts.title: It Protects By Sacrificing Itself
facts.text: Zinc is more chemically reactive than iron, so when steel is coated in zinc (galvanizing), the zinc corrodes first and shields the iron underneath. This is called sacrificial or cathodic protection, and it works even where the coating is scratched, because the surrounding zinc keeps giving up electrons. Roughly half of all the zinc mined each year goes into galvanizing to stop steel from rusting.

facts.title: A Spark In Your Brain
facts.text: Zinc is the second most abundant trace metal in the human body after iron, and an adult carries about 2 to 3 grams of it. It is a structural or catalytic component of hundreds of enzymes and of the "zinc finger" proteins that grip DNA to switch genes on and off. In the brain, neurons store zinc in synaptic vesicles and release it during signaling, making it essential for memory and learning.

facts.title: The Original Battery Metal
facts.text: When Alessandro Volta built the first true battery, the voltaic pile of 1800, he stacked discs of zinc and copper separated by brine-soaked cloth. Zinc readily gives up electrons, so it still serves as the negative electrode in everyday alkaline and zinc-carbon batteries. Zinc-air cells, which pull oxygen straight from the atmosphere, power most modern hearing aids.

facts.title: Brass Came Before Pure Zinc
facts.text: Humans used zinc in alloys long before they could make the pure metal. Brass, an alloy of copper and zinc, was produced by the Romans by heating copper with zinc ore (calamine) and charcoal, a trick that dissolved the zinc without ever isolating it. Adding zinc to copper makes brass harder, more golden, and far easier to cast and machine than copper alone.

facts.title: The Healing Mineral
facts.text: Zinc oxide is the white, opaque paste in sunscreens and diaper creams, where it physically blocks ultraviolet light and soothes irritated skin. Adequate zinc is critical for wound healing and a working immune system, and the World Health Organization recommends zinc supplements to treat childhood diarrhea in developing countries. Severe deficiency causes a rare disease called acrodermatitis enteropathica, marked by skin lesions and stunted growth.

facts.title: Forged In Dying Stars
facts.text: Zinc is built inside massive stars and scattered across the galaxy when they explode as supernovae. Astronomers actually use zinc to measure pollution of the early universe, because unlike iron it is barely absorbed onto interstellar dust grains, so it faithfully tracks how much heavy-element "metal" a distant gas cloud truly contains. The Sun and the wider cosmos contain only trace amounts, making zinc a relatively rare element compared with the iron it so often guards.

facts.title: Cold Snap, Brittle Metal
facts.text: Zinc has a surprising mechanical personality that depends sharply on temperature. At room temperature cast zinc is fairly brittle, but between about 100 and 150 C it becomes soft and malleable enough to roll into sheets, then turns brittle again above roughly 210 C. Because its melting point is a low 420 C, zinc is easy to die-cast into intricate shapes for car parts, hardware, and toys.

facts.title: Pennies Are Mostly Zinc
facts.text: Since 1982 the United States one-cent coin has been made of 97.5 percent zinc with only a thin copper plating, because copper had become too expensive to mint. So while a penny looks coppery, it is really a zinc slug wearing a copper coat. Zinc's affordability and the ease of plating it make this kind of disguise a common industrial trick.
